subjects.displayTitle: Food and diet: gratitude at the table
subjects.introduction: Hunger satisfied with thankfulness is, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, a divine standard, and the plate in front of us turns out to be a fair place to ask what mercy, freedom and fellowship require. He teaches that the human body was not built for a carnivore’s life, that a lamb’s feelings are as real as our own, and that contentment with grain, fruit, oil and nuts is closer to compassion; yet he laughs off requests for a prescribed regimen, allows meat where health or habit requires it, and notes that the Prophets withhold a prohibition people could not yet bear. The subject refuses to become a badge of superiority. Paul, writing to the Romans about believers who ate differently, asked each side to stop despising and judging the other [1], and the same spirit shows in the hospitality offered to a guest whose religion shaped what he could eat. Stories of potatoes and unfamiliar tastes show how slowly habits move. From the table the inquiry widens into health and healing, the hope that medicine will one day work through food, and the kindness owed to animals.
subjects.arc: Begin with gratitude and mercy, explore freedom and habit, and finish with hospitality, bodily explanations, and a small story of moderation.

order.why: Extend gratitude into compassion for animals. Consider the fuller argument connecting diet with mercy.
shortened: Regarding the eating of animal flesh and abstinence therefrom, know thou of a certainty that, in the beginning of creation, God determined the food of every living being, and to eat contrary to that determination is not approved.

Truly, the killing of animals and the eating of their meat is somewhat contrary to pity and compassion, and if one can content oneself with cereals, fruit, oil and nuts, such as pistachios, almonds and so on, it would undoubtedly be better and more pleasing.

order.why: Let an ordinary meal open the spiritual inquiry.
Distinguish compassion from claims of intellectual superiority.
shortened: Question: What is the relative effect of vegetable and animal foods upon the mind of man or spirit of man?

'Abdu'l-Baha said: "It has no effect. It does not develop the mind to subsist upon a vegetable diet. A man can be without reason or understanding, though he does not eat meat or flesh, and again one eats flesh but his mind is very sharp.

"The more man avoids hurting the animal the better. It is very strange that a man should kill an animal for his food, but since meat is in the market one buys it. It is indeed very grievous to kill a lamb or other animal for one's food, for the feelings of an animal are just as great as our own.

order.why: Hold permission and mercy together.
Introduce humor about requests for a prescribed diet.
Make the question tangible through a shared vegetarian meal.
shortened: While I was in America one of the believers by the name Mon. Bourgeois of New York City who is a vegetarian invited me to dinner. Such nutritious dishes were prepared with nuts and vegetables and rice that any one could easily dispense with meat-eating. I said to Mon and Madame Bourgeois of you can concoct such delicious dishes with vegetables and nuts I can assure you many people will join your crusade against slaughtering animals and eating their flesh.

order.why: Consider tenderness alongside the practical circumstances of food.
shortened: If one should wholly abstain from meat and be contented with vegetables, it would be much better. And how difficult it is for a man to kill an animal and to prepare the food for himself. But as it is already killed and we find it in the market, we buy it.
If the people could bear it, the prophets would prohibit the eating of flesh.

order.why: Acknowledge the influence of established habits.
Read another brief counsel about preference and habit.
Place a historical explanation beside the explicit absence of prohibition. Revisit permission in the separately supplied excerpt.
Examine the anatomical reasoning used in the reported discussion.
Explains the expectation that consumption of meat will gradually diminish as humanity develops.

sourceQuestion.text: Question: What will be the food of the united people?

order.why: Broaden the inquiry to hopes for the relation of food and healing. Read the extended explanation of food and bodily balance.
shortened: The Bab hath said that the people of Baha must develop the science of medicine to such a high degree that they will heal illnesses by means of foods.

At whatever time highly skilled physicians shall have developed the healing of illnesses by means of foods, and shall make provision for simple foods, and shall prohibit humankind from living as slaves to their lustful appetites, it is certain that the incidence of chronic and diversified illnesses will abate, and the general health of all mankind will be much improved. This is destined to come about.

order.why: Show how cultural resistance can shape food choices.
shortened: This kind of food is not Persian. It is European, except that there is one Persian dish - the sweetened rice. At first there were no potatoes in Persia. This is something new with the Persians-imported from Europe. At first the Persians did not take kindly to the potato, saying it was an apple of Europe, because of their fanaticism.

order.why: See hospitality accommodate a guest’s religious practice.
shortened: I said, "What is kosher that you may eat? Is bread kosher?" He said yes. I said, "Are sugar, water and lemon juice kosher?" He said yes. I said, "Are eggs kosher?" He said, "If I boil them, yes they are kosher." They brought a coffee pot and I gave him boiled eggs to eat. He said, "I must boil them myself." They boiled the coffee pot again and he himself cooked the eggs and ate them.

order.why: Return the linked readings to the spiritual meaning of nourishment.
Read the discussion of necessity and bodily condition.
shortened: But eating meat is not forbidden or unlawful, nay, the point is this, that it is possible for man to live without eating meat and still be strong. Meat is nourishing and containeth the elements of herbs, seeds and fruits; therefore sometimes it is essential for the sick and for the rehabilitation of health. There is no objection in the Law of God to the eating of meat if it is required. So if thy constitution is rather weak and thou findest meat useful, thou mayest eat it.

order.why: Explore the longer reported account of habit and physiology.
shortened: 'Abdu'l-Baha said, "If someone has never eaten meat and is not used to it, even passing by a butcher shop, the smell of meat is so bad and offensive that it disturbs them. But those who are accustomed to it hardly notice." And the Blessed Beauty, considering that humanity has become accustomed to eating meat and it has become very common, did not forbid it, but said "humans were not created to be meat-eaters."

order.why: Consider the reported hope for future dietary change.

questions: How might gratitude change the way a person obtains, prepares, shares, or consumes food?
What distinction do these readings draw between showing mercy to animals and making diet a measure of another person’s spiritual worth?
How does the account of accommodating a guest’s food practice illuminate Paul’s counsel about judgment in Romans 14?
What do the stories about potatoes, familiar tastes, and shared meals suggest about how habits change?
How could moderation, hospitality, and compassion guide a conversation in which people make different dietary choices?

neighbors.invitation: Follow the image of pure water and a clean cup into the spiritual meaning of ordinary care.
Explore moderation that permits enjoyment while discouraging self-imposed hardship.

references.label: 1 · Romans 14:2–4 · Food and mutual regard
references.note: Paul addresses differing practices around food and asks both sides to refrain from contempt and judgment. Compare the concern for fellowship with the hospitality and freedom of choice in these selections; the passage is not a statement of Bahá’í dietary law.

subjects.displayTitle: Cleanliness: care for the visible and invisible
subjects.introduction: Wear your purest garments, the Báb instructs a visitor, not your most splendid ones: refinement begins with care rather than cost. The Bahá’í writings treat cleanliness as something more than hygiene and less than vanity. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá pictures the streambed that must be cleansed before sweet water can be led into it, so that purity of surroundings and purity of character answer each other, and He calls the body the temple of the spirit, to be kept clean because of what it houses. Bahá’u’lláh is concrete: hands out of the common dish, no trace of dirt on a garment, houses washed, and refinement loved in all conditions, while reasonable excuse is always allowed. The theme reaches into hospitality, a traveller’s room, a public bathhouse built as an act of service, even a properly made cup of tea; and the Báb widens it into a principle of making, that whoever has power over a thing must raise it to its own perfection. The Qur’án joins washing before prayer with gratitude and an express wish to lay no hardship on anyone [1]. The road continues toward beauty and the arts, toward courtesy and the culture of adab, and toward health and healing.
subjects.arc: Begin with accessible refinement, connect body and character, then move through hospitality, changing purity rules, beauty, and kindness.

order.why: Use the streambed to connect outward and inward purity.
Open with the clean old shirt rather than costly appearance.
Set enduring virtues beside visible garments.
shortened: "Thou art right, the believers of God must ever strive to clothe their spiritual bodies with the garment of the virtue of God, the robe of the fear of God, and the vesture of the love of God. These robes will never become threadbare.
"But the outward raiment must be also clean and immaculate, so that the outer may be a faint expression of the inner. Cleanliness is one of the fundamental laws of this religion."

order.why: Consider the body as a spiritual temple.
shortened: It is well expressed that cleanliness is godliness; because this body is the spiritual temple of the Almighty. It must be kept clean and pure. Physical and spiritual cleanliness are intimately associated with each other.

order.why: Read the direct counsel on food, garments, and reasonable excuse.
shortened: Take heed lest, when partaking of food, ye plunge your hands into the contents of bowls and platters. Adopt ye such usages as are most in keeping with refinement. He, verily, desireth to see in you the manners of the inmates of Paradise in His mighty and most sublime Kingdom. Hold ye fast unto refinement under all conditions, that your eyes may be preserved from beholding what is repugnant both to your own selves and to the dwellers of Paradise. Should anyone depart therefrom, his deed shall at that moment be rendered vain; yet should he have good reason, God will excuse him.
Cleave ye unto the cord of refinement with such tenacity as to allow no trace of dirt to be seen upon your garments.

order.why: Bring care into the home.
shortened: Cleanse your houses, O people, and wash your garments of whatsoever is abhorrent unto God. Thus doth the All-Knowing counsel you. We love refinement in all conditions.

order.why: Notice the effect of pleasant surroundings.
Extend that care to travelers.
Make cleanliness a form of public service through the bathhouse.
Concentrate the theme in the image of a cup of tea.
shortened: Tea must be like this: good sugar, excellent tea, purified water, clean cup and in every way neat and organized. Otherwise, it is better not to drink it.

order.why: Connect habits of care with joy.
Return to garments and spiritual life.
Explore refinement through imagery associated with the Báb.
shortened: The Concourse on High and the sanctified spirits have their gaze fixed upon perfumed, pure and refined stations. Thus did the Herald declare that prayer offered in silk garments is more excellent before God. Likewise He said that if He knew which place thou wouldst choose as thy residence, He would even now command that it be built of diamond faces reflecting water.

order.why: Read the Báb’s further counsel in its own setting.
Notice the qualification of ability in the supplied passage. End with kindness to oneself and others as the purpose of care.
shortened: Therefore cleanse what ye wear with water as soon as ye are able, that ye may find the mercy of your Lord within yourselves and be thankful.

Therefore show ye mercy one to another and be ye kind to yourselves insofar as ye are able, and adorn yourselves for God your Lord through your glorification of God and your remembrance of His praise, and through your magnification of God and your remembrance of His oneness, and through your wearing of the finest raiment ye possess. This is of God's grace and mercy towards you, that ye may be thankful.

order.why: Answers a practical question about used washing water and explicitly identifies cleanliness as the purpose.
Read the further counsel about garments and fragrance.
Distinguish a disputed purity teaching from its attributed source.
Retain the historical reported criticism without making it a general description of a people.
Consider the reported relation between bodily state and spiritual expression. Read the concise statement of cleanliness as a religious foundation.
Broaden refinement into beauty, proportion, and art.
shortened: It is natural for the heart and spirit to take pleasure and enjoyment in all things that show forth symmetry, harmony, and perfection. For instance: a beautiful house, a well designed garden, a symmetrical line, a graceful motion, a well written book, pleasing garments—in fact, all things that have in themselves grace or beauty are pleasing to the heart and spirit—therefore, it is most certain that a true voice causes deep pleasure.

order.why: Explore the image of each thing attaining its paradise. Consider the responsibility implied by excellence in making things.
shortened: Rather, He hath commanded a universal precept for all things, that whoever possesseth power over anything, must elevate that thing to its uttermost perfection, that it would not be deprived of its own paradise.

For each thing, within its own station, yearneth to attain unto the utmost height of excellence in its own level. Thus, when a man is in a position of power to realise its yearning, and he faileth to do so, he would be held accountable therefor.

questions: What does the preference for an old clean shirt reveal about the difference between refinement and display?
How do the streambed and garment images connect physical surroundings with character without making outward appearance a sufficient measure of goodness?
How might care for a visitor, a shared room, or public facilities become a form of spiritual service?
What similarities and differences emerge when the Qur’an’s washing, gratitude, and accommodation of hardship are read beside these selections?
How could the Báb’s image of the perfection of things influence the way we make, maintain, or share ordinary objects?

neighbors.invitation: Consider refinement together with the explicit recognition that poverty is an excuse.
Explore how improving an artistic skill can be understood as worship.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 5:6 · Washing, gratitude, and ease
references.note: The verse prescribes washing before prayer, provides an alternative when water is unavailable in specified circumstances, and connects purification with gratitude rather than intended hardship. Compare its ritual setting with the wider care for body and surroundings in this compilation.

subjects.introduction: Let your eye be chaste, your hand faithful, your tongue truthful and your heart enlightened. In Bahá’u’lláh’s sentence chastity is one strand in a whole person made trustworthy, inseparable from fidelity and honest speech. It is asked of everyone: a woman who sought a new companion each day would be judged unchaste, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that the same is true for men. Strength is redefined along the way, since a man of elephantine physique can be weaker than an ant while a woman behind the veil of purity may be the very picture of power, noble through reason and restraint. Marriage appears as a fortress, girls are to be taught constancy and firmness of purpose, and an atom of chastity is said to outweigh an ocean of knowledge. The Qur’an addresses men first [1] and then women [2] in its call to guard the gaze, a comparison that shows shared responsibility together with differing rules and settings. Shoghi Effendi’s account of a chaste and holy life reaches into dress, speech and amusements, and ends in forbearance toward others. The path continues toward purity of heart, the mastery of lust and passion, and sincerity of intention.
subjects.arc: Open with integrated character, test assumptions about strength and gender, explore education and devotion, then end with public integrity and personal forbearance.

order.why: Open with the memorable image of a trustworthy whole person.
shortened: Let your eye be chaste, your hand faithful, your tongue truthful and your heart enlightened.

order.why: Confront the double standard early.
shortened: If a woman were to seek a new bed-companion each day this behavior would be evidence of complete unchastity. When thou considerest it truly, it is the same for men.

order.why: Redefine strength through mastery of desire.
shortened: For we observe that a male person with an elephant-like physique can be as lowly, contemptible and weak as an ant, while behind the veil of chastity and purity, a female can be the epitome of strength and power - the former enslaved by self and passion, the latter noble through reason and restraint; the former sinful and the latter virtuous.

order.why: Establish the summons to all.
Join chastity with trustworthiness.
shortened: Say: O concourse of loved ones! Hold fast unto trustworthiness, chastity and faithfulness.

order.why: Place kindliness alongside steadfastness and restraint.
shortened: We counsel all to manifest the most great steadfastness, and chastity, and trustworthiness, and faithfulness, and that kindliness which We have enjoined upon all in My Most Great Book.

order.why: Read the direct exhortation to purity.
shortened: And in another connection these words were revealed: "We enjoin the servants of God and His handmaidens to be pure and to fear God, that they may shake off the slumber of their corrupt desires, and turn toward God, the Maker of the heavens and of the earth.

order.why: Consider chastity in relation to recognition of God.
Explore the protective image of marriage.
Keep a reported discussion of customs in its cultural setting.
shortened: He continued: "Women and men must not embrace each other when not married, or not about to be married. They must not kiss each other.
The Blessed Beauty directed that there should be great modesty in the women, that they should not bare the neck and bosom, and that the women in the East should wear a veil.

"The conditions are different in the West, but the women of the West must see the spiritual significance of this teaching. Do not distress them by saying that they should not have done this or that. They will see by themselves. Talk about this only, so to speak, one by one, with the friends, when you have opportunity."

order.why: Move to the education of girls.
shortened: And further, those present should concern themselves with every means of training the girl children; with teaching the various branches of knowledge, good behaviour, a proper way of life, the cultivation of a good character, chastity and constancy, perseverance, strength, determination, firmness of purpose; with household management, the education of children, and whatever especially applieth to the needs of girls -- to the end that these girls, reared in the stronghold of all perfections, and with the protection of a goodly character, will, when they themselves become mothers, bring up their children from earliest infancy to have a good character and conduct themselves well.

order.why: Connect education with the cultivation of virtue.
shortened: Become a manifestation of bounty and the essence of sanctification, detachment and supreme purity. Teach the sign of chastity and in the school of handmaidens give lessons in infinite virtue.

order.why: Maintains chastity while affirming that it must not obstruct women’s education and acquisition of virtues.
Hold purity and knowledge together.
Continue the connection with knowledge and perfection.
shortened: Therefore they must arise to that which befits this station and is worthy of this glory - namely, purity and detachment, radiance and sanctification, chastity and holiness, spirituality and cleanliness, perfection and knowledge, detachment and luminosity.

order.why: Consider character as a source of enduring honor.
Explore the image of adornment.
shortened: Say: The greatest ornament for the handmaidens hath ever been and still is chastity and virtue. By God! The light of chastity illumineth the horizons of the spiritual worlds and its fragrance reacheth unto the Most Exalted Paradise.

order.why: Read the complementary image of a crown.
shortened: God hath made chastity a crown for the heads of His handmaidens. Blessed is the handmaiden who hath attained unto this mighty station.

order.why: Hear the further counsel addressed to women.
Join chastity with steadfastness.
Consider virtue as a publicly raised banner.
Read encouragement amid persecution.
shortened: But the essences of chastity and modesty, that is, the women who are faithful to God and assured in Him, though they experience injustice and persecution, sustain injuries and tribulations, become the objects of pillage and plunder, and behold their own loved ones spill their blood drop by drop upon the earth at the altar of love, these in the end shall receive the reward of eternal life, dwell in the Kingdom of heaven, experience infinite gladness, and enjoy everlasting gifts.

order.why: Make room for consolation in grief.
shortened: O My handmaiden! Grieve not at what hath befallen thee, but hold fast unto purity, that the people of Paradise may inhale from thee the sweet fragrance of holiness.

order.why: Explore the relation of inward purity and expressive power.
shortened: All pure things are acceptable. For example: water-pure-is acceptable; fresh air is most acceptable. As all pure things are acceptable and pleasing, therefore a pure voice is most acceptable, and causes great enjoyment.

There are two kinds of voices. One when the complete instrument is perfect, then the emission of sound is perfect. The second is when the instrument is imperfect, it affects the voice in such a way that is far from pleasing.

order.why: Gather the theme in the image of two standards.
shortened: Chastity and purity of life are the two divine standards of the spiritual and moral law.

order.why: Connect bodily care and inward life.
shortened: The body and the spirit alike must be kept clean and pure; in order to become in the image and likeness of God. let your watchword be 'clean bodies, pure spirits'.

order.why: Close the linked readings with prayer.
Retain the supplied fragment concerning desire.
Read the counsel about gaze in its supplied form.
shortened: The people of Baha must be manifestations of the greatest chastity and supreme virtue. In the divine texts it is written, and the meaning of the verse in Persian is that even if the most beautiful women were to pass before them, their gaze would never turn in that direction. The meaning is that purity and sanctity are among the greatest characteristics of the people of Baha.
For an atom of chastity is greater than a hundred thousand years of worship and an ocean of knowledge.

order.why: Test integrity through images of wealth and attraction.
Return to marriage as a fortress.
Include the reported appreciation of a nun’s humility and prayer.
Read the broader account of a chaste and holy life.
shortened: A chaste and holy life must be made the controlling principle in the behavior and conduct of all Baha'is, both in their social relations with the members of their own community, and in their contact with the world at large.... Such a chaste and holy life, with its implications of modesty, purity, temperance, decency, and clean-mindedness, involves no less than the exercise of moderation in all that pertains to dress, language, amusements, and all artistic and literary avocations. It demands daily vigilance in the control of one's carnal desires and corrupt inclinations. It calls for the abandonment of a frivolous conduct, with its excessive attachment to trivial and often misdirected pleasures.

order.why: Connect personal integrity with justice and freedom from racial prejudice.
End with conscience and uncensorious forbearance.

questions: How does the opening image of eye, hand, tongue, and heart enlarge the meaning of chastity?
What does the rejection of a double standard require of the ways men and women are educated, praised, or held responsible?
How might restraint become a form of strength that also protects tenderness and trust?
What does reading the Qur’an’s addresses to men and women alongside these selections reveal about shared responsibilities and differing religious prescriptions?
How can a person pursue a demanding standard for their own conduct while practicing the forbearance urged in the final selection?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the moral influence of theater alongside the encouragement of artistic expression.
Explore the distinction between outward garments and enduring inward virtues.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 24:30 · Address to men
references.note: This verse calls believing men to guard their gaze and chastity. Read it with the following verse and compare the shared responsibility with the compilation’s rejection of a sexual double standard.

references.label: 2 · Qur’an 24:31 · Address to women
references.note: The next verse addresses women, adds detailed prescriptions about adornment and covering, and ends with a collective call to repentance. Compare the common ethical concern while preserving the differences between the religious settings and their specific rules.

subjects.displayTitle: Monasticism and asceticism: a life turned toward others
subjects.introduction: People must live for one another, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, and not shut themselves away as monks and nuns do. Seclusion and asceticism are not acceptable before God, Bahá’u’lláh declares, and those with insight should pursue what brings joy and radiance. The reason is not contempt for discipline but a judgment about its fruit. A person weakened by exaggerated fasting or shut in a dark cell may be free of covetousness, yet the freedom comes from the atrophy of his powers. The same writings honour the thousands of noble daughters who exchanged silk for the coarse habit, and praise the nuns who labour in hospitals. Benedict’s Rule, with its hours of work, prayer and rest and its allowance for the frail, shows that monastic life was never simply idleness, even where the Bahá’í teachings part from the vocation itself [1]. The believer is asked to work, to enjoy the lawful blessings of life, and to guard the strength service requires. The journey continues into useful occupation and into the truth that no one can live alone.
subjects.arc: Begin with service and gratitude, examine the meaning and limits of austerity, honor dedication, and end with concrete counsels on moderation and rest.

order.why: Open with the positive purpose of living for one another.
shortened: People must live for one another, and not live in seclusion as do the monks and nuns. People should not live solitary lives.

order.why: Ground service in gratitude for life.
shortened: If we hold enmity with life, we are ingrates, for our material and spiritual existence is the outward evidences of the divine mercy.

order.why: Establish joy and radiance as an alternative to withdrawal. Return to the call for joy.
Make the alternative concrete through healthy work and service.
Read the parallel emphasis on useful occupation.
Distinguish hospital service from seclusion in the account of nuns.
Reconsider how spiritual perfection is pursued.
Explore discipline that preserves rather than weakens spiritual powers.
shortened: Physical asceticism will in the course of time cause an absolute atrophy of the parts, resulting in the greatest weakness. There will be no love of transgression, no attachment to this life, no covetousness, no aggressiveness, but all this is due to great weakness of powers. But spiritual asceticism will help one to attain to such blossoming of powers as will help one to attain to make up his mind against the things that are not to be and will encourage him in the things to be.
In this Dispensation there is no physical or material asceticism.

order.why: Consider the cost of exaggerated fasting.
shortened: Exaggerated fasting destroys the divine forces. God has created man in a way that cannot be surpassed; we must not try to change his creation.

order.why: Set refinement and charity beside the explicit excuse of poverty.
shortened: But some among the Shi'ite sect maintain their dwellings and attire in an unrefined state and consider this asceticism and the very essence of piety. Indeed, if these conditions arise from poverty, there is no harm in it and it is acceptable before God. But when means are available, whatsoever they manifest or bestow in charity is beloved in the sight of God.

order.why: Acknowledge the dedication of those who leave privilege.
shortened: O handmaidens of the All-Merciful and pure, assured, confident leaves through God's grace!

Thousands upon thousands of daughters of kings and children of nobles and great ones abandoned silk and brocade, forsook comfort and peace of soul and heart's desire and adornment, turned away from father and mother, detached themselves from every joy and happiness and pleasure, donned the garment of monasticism to become nuns, and spent their days and nights in worship and austerity and solitude and supplication - that perhaps they might witness a ray of the light of truth.

order.why: Read the account of hardship sought by mystics.
Introduce the relation between austerity and grace.
shortened: To Mr. and Mrs. Schweizer convey my respectful greetings and say that the monks who spent years upon years in mountains and wilderness in monasteries and who imagined they were worshipping God and spent their days in austerity - they were the people who were called but you who underwent no hardship were chosen through pure divine bounty.

order.why: Read the parallel address concerning grace.
Continue the contrast between effort and unearned bounty.
shortened: O ye pure handmaidens of the Blessed Beauty! Praised and glorified be God that ye have attained the stations of nearness to the All-Glorious, while many ascetics and devotees, who take no account of the time of the day, consecrate themselves to the Adored One in the mosques and monasteries with heads constantly bowed in worship, and numerous holy women and nuns seclude themselves by renouncing the world and live in a state of continual fasting, have not.

order.why: Retain the reported description of enclosed cells.
Read the stronger criticism within its reported setting.
Return to work among one’s fellows.
Turn from withdrawal toward the call to recognition.
Explore the difference between attachment to a name and recognition of its bearer.
Close the linked sequence with the monk and the bell.
shortened: O Monk of the Divine Unity! Ring out the bell, for the Day of the Lord is come and the Beauty of the All-Glorious hath ascended His blessed and resplendent throne.

order.why: Read the Báb’s provision concerning monasticism.
Question the idea that austerity itself secures divine acceptance.
shortened: Were anyone to wash the feet of all mankind, and were he to worship God in the forests, valleys, and mountains, upon high hills and lofty peaks, to leave no rock or tree, no clod of earth, but was a witness to his worship--yet, should the fragrance of My good pleasure not be inhaled from him, his works would never be acceptable unto God.

How many a man hath secluded himself in the climes of India, denied himself the things that God hath decreed as lawful, imposed upon himself austerities and mortifications, and hath not been remembered by God, the Revealer of Verses. Make not your deeds as snares wherewith to entrap the object of your aspiration, and deprive not yourselves of this Ultimate Objective for which have ever yearned all such as have drawn nigh unto God.

order.why: Read the further supplied criticism of seclusion.
shortened: Consider these nuns. ('Abdu'l-Baha pointed to several nuns that were passing by.) They are not aware of the teachings of Christ, nor of His ordinances, and indeed are ignorant of everything. But in following their own vain imaginings are in fact performing these sacrificial deeds. They withdraw from society and normal life and live in these convents.

order.why: Continue the critique in its original terms.
Notice remembrance of monks’ deeds alongside the call to enter the world. Read the parallel passage from the Glad-Tidings.
Distinguish exclusive dedication to service from a monastic institution.
shortened: Another blessed talk was about divine confirmation and heavenly blessing, culminating in these words (addressing one of the friends who worked in a monastic administration):

There is no monasticism in this Cause, but a person who wishes to devote his time exclusively to teaching the Cause of God and serving the human race can still distance himself from the things of this world. It would certainly be preferable for him to spend his time in service to the Kingdom of God, but not to practise monasticism.

order.why: Explicitly distinguishes spiritual growth through virtue and divine favor from extreme asceticism and monasticism.
Clarify the renunciation of self-centered desire while enjoying blessings.
Reject self-imposed hardship as a measure of devotion.
Locate the subject within the supplied account of institutional change.
Introduce balance between resources, service, and personal growth.
Consider protecting health and reserves of strength.
shortened: The Baha'is, in spite of their self-sacrificing desire to give the last drop of their strength to serving the Cause, must guard against utterly depleting their forces and having breakdowns.

If you take better care of your own health, and build up your reserves, it would certainly be better for you and for your work. Then your sensitive, yearning heart, although you may still often suffer for and with others, will be better able to withstand its trials, and you will not get so exhausted, which is certainly no asset to your work for the Cause.

order.why: End with rest and the memorable image of caring for one’s mount.

questions: How does living for others change the meaning of sacrifice or renunciation?
What distinction emerges between criticism of seclusion and appreciation for the devotion and hospital service of nuns?
How does Benedict’s arrangement of work, reading, and rest complicate the comparison between monastic and Bahá’í forms of spiritual life?
What helps distinguish a discipline that strengthens service from an austerity that diminishes the person’s capacity to serve?
How might the final counsels about moderation, enjoyment, and rest change the way a community encourages dedication?

neighbors.invitation: Explore gratitude within the ordinary act of eating.
Consider refinement that values a clean old garment over costly display.

references.note: Benedict arranges manual labor, sacred reading, and rest within monastic life, and asks that work be adapted for the sick or fragile. Compare this balance with the compilation’s service and moderation while recognizing the difference concerning the monastic vocation itself.

subjects.displayTitle: The arts: giving form to possibility
subjects.introduction: A poem can carry a fresh meaning into the heart before the mind has found words to explain it, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks poets for exactly that: new meanings, sweeter rhythm, words worthy of the light they bear. Human nature, He says, is moved more by verse than by prose. Yet inspiration is paired with study, and praise of a ghazal sits beside the charge to finish school and master composition. Painting is set a high aim too, to reflect the forms of the Concourse on High in the mirror of the world below, and drama is credited with the power to educate feeling. Aristotle’s claim that poetry explores what could happen rather than what did offers a fruitful comparison [1], for both accounts hold that imagined particulars can disclose real patterns. Reverence draws a boundary at representing the Manifestations of God in paint or on stage, and that limit says something about what art is for. The path continues into creativity in art, into music and singing, and into the newer arts of photography and recording.
subjects.arc: Begin with fresh meaning and emotional power, deepen the practice of craft, explore theater and visual art, then consider reverence and representation.

order.why: Consider why poetry can affect the heart.
shortened: Human nature is more affected by poetry than prose. Poems have a different influence, and odes and lyrics have another radiance.

I hope that you will progress to such a degree that you will surpass the poets of old and acquire complete mastery in all forms of poetry, becoming a nightingale of meanings and a dove in the divine garden.

order.why: Open with the discovery of fresh meaning.
Connect poetry with the art of expression.
Ground inspiration in study.
shortened: You had asked about my wish - my purpose is that you study the sciences and knowledge, acquire the art of poetry and composition, complete your studies in school, raise the call to the Kingdom, and engage in spreading the lights of truth.

order.why: Extend cultivated expression into cooperation and service.
Make improvement tangible through rhythm and content.
Read praise of an ode’s eloquence and innovation.
Notice expression across several languages.
Attend to the beauty of the ghazal.
Enter the extended imagery of the nightingale.
Explore meaning through the image of flowers.
Consider the value assigned to each word.
Reflect on simplicity that is difficult to achieve.

Read the image of a shared source of inspiration.
Hold acquired skill and spiritual inspiration together.
shortened: Art without the subtle music of the spirit which is only heard by the still small voice; art without the spiritual inspiration of the higher spheres; art without the infinite waves and vibrations of the super-human; art without the tender messages of the anemones and hyacinths of the spiritual rose-garden is not art but artifice. Therefore you must make an effort to master both branches of Art.

order.why: Consider art practiced as worship.
Explore painting and ideal form.
shortened: Now if that one intoxicated with the divine cup seeks complete proficiency in the art of drawing and illustration, he must strive until the image of the Concourse on High is reflected in the mirror of the world below, and those celestial forms draw back the veil in every realm of the material world.
If the contingent world becomes confirmed with this gift of the All-Merciful, then this world will become a Most Glorious Paradise.

order.why: Develop the relation of the visible world to a heavenly pattern.
Read the world through the image of a written book.
shortened: O Calligrapher! This world of being is an inscribed book and an unfurled scroll. If thou art able, write with majestic pen upon this contingent page the praises and attributes of the Blessed Beauty, and record in the mighty tablet of creation unique odes and the qualities of the Most Great Luminary, that thou mayest behold the Preserved Tablet and witness the inscriptions of the Mother Book.

order.why: Turn artistic imagery toward deeds.
shortened: Can you paint upon the page of the world the ideal pictures of the Supreme Concourse The pictures which are in the ideal world are eternal. I desire you to become such an Artist.
Man can paint those ideal pictures upon the Tablet of existence with the brush of deeds.

order.why: Open the question of theater’s moral influence.
Consider theater as a school of feeling.
Read the concise claim for drama’s power.
shortened: "The drama is of the utmost importance." said Abdu'l-Baha. "It has been a great educational power in the past; it will be so again."

order.why: Explore a concrete dramatic outline of awakening.
shortened: The Herald of the Kingdom stands before the people. Wonderful music swells from an unseen orchestra, moving and soul-inspiring. The music becomes soft while the Herald proclaims the coming of the Kingdom. He holds a trumpet to his mouth. The curtain rises. The stage is crowded with men and women; all are asleep. At the sound of the trumpet they begin to awake.

order.why: Follow poetry across cultural boundaries through Saadi and Hafiz.
Consider the reported contrast in the reception of painting.
Retain the historical account of grave carvings as a reported explanation.
Return to encouragement offered to a poet.
Read the separately supplied praise of poetry.
shortened: Verily, these verse shall be sung in the divine meetings and in the assemblages of the spiritual in the course of ages and centuries to come, for thou hast uttered the praise of thy Lord and expressed significant meanings in eulogy of thy Lord, the Merciful, the Clement. All poems shall be forgotten in the course of time save those that are extraordinary; thy poem shall be chanted with melody and best voices in the Center of Worship (or Mashrak-el-Azcar) forevermore.

order.why: Appreciates eloquent poetry as flowing water and a feast of truths and meanings.
Examine the distinction between historical drama and portraying central sacred figures.
End with the further clarification on reverence and artistic representation.
shortened: The prohibition on representing the Manifestation of God in paintings and drawings or in dramatic presentations applies to all the Manifestations of God. There are, of course, great and wonderful works of art of past Dispensations, many of which portrayed the Manifestations of God in a spirit of reverence and love. In this Dispensation however the greater maturity of mankind and the greater awareness of the relationship between the Supreme Manifestation and His servants enable us to realize the impossibility of representing, in any human form, whether pictorially, in sculpture or in dramatic representation, the Person of God's Manifestations.

How do these selections connect inspiration with the patient development of skill?
What becomes possible when art is understood as an act of worship or service, and what questions does that understanding raise for the artist?

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Poetics IX · What might happen
references.note: In Part IX, Aristotle distinguishes the poet’s exploration of possible action from the historian’s account of particular events. Compare this account of art’s reach with the selections on drama and spiritual inspiration, without treating the two theories of artistic purpose as identical.

subjects.introduction: Persia once gave the world sciences, arts and a model of just kingship; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes it may now give the light of spiritual civilization. That hope sets the tone for a reckoning with inheritance. The ancient kings of Iran prided themselves on justice rather than jewelled crowns; Bukhara was once a wellspring of learning; the Parsis are addressed as a noble people whose crown has been renewed. Beside these appeals stand accounts of desert simplicity, a Bedouin woman who scorns the city’s cage-like houses, and reported contrasts between Eastern devotion and Western detachment that speak in the rhetoric of their moment rather than as verdicts on whole peoples. The Qur’an’s reminder that peoples and tribes were made so that they might know one another, with honour resting in righteousness, keeps the difference between cherishing a heritage and claiming superiority in view [1]. From here the journey widens into the meeting of East and West, into the hopes placed in Japan and China, and into the past, present and future of Iran itself.
subjects.arc: Begin with cultural gifts offered to others, explore memory and renewal, consider simplicity and poetic life, and return to exchange across societies.

order.why: Describes the complementary material and spiritual civilizations of West and East and the benefit of their union.
Explore the appeal to Persian history as a call to renewal.
shortened: She was distinguished among all peoples for the scope of her dominion, she was honored by all for her praiseworthy culture and civilization. She was as the pivot of the world, she was the source and center of sciences and arts, the wellspring of great inventions and discoveries, the rich mine of human virtues and perfections. The intellect, the wisdom of the individual members of this excellent nation dazzled the minds of other peoples, the brilliance and perceptive genius that characterized all this noble race aroused the envy of the whole world.

order.why: Set decline in learning beside remembered achievement.
Ask what gives a ruler lasting honor.
Reinterpret inherited images of royal greatness.
Give cultural attachment a personal voice.
shortened: Even though it has been sixty years since I left Iran, I am still not content that even a minor Iranian custom be abandoned.
The Baha'is adore Iran - and this is not just talk.

order.why: Read the connection between renewal and tested faith.
shortened: For praise be to God, Iran is the planted field of the Blessed Tree and the dawning-place of the Most Great Light, and the friends are veterans who were raised in the shadow of the Blessed Beauty's training - they are tested and self-sacrificing, each one's ultimate desire being the field of martyrdom.

order.why: Continue the hope for spiritual illumination.
shortened: Otherwise the light of truth shone from the horizon of Iran, the luminary of the horizons rose in that blessed land, and the beloved of love illumined its face in that gathering, and the melody of the Abha Kingdom was raised from that luminous land.

order.why: Include the appeal to Zoroastrian communities.
shortened: O Zoroastrian friends! Every people among the peoples had their day of triumph, and on that day they held great festivities and established feasts of joy and delight. Today is your day, it is your time of joy and gladness, for the Persian Sun hath shone forth from the horizon of Iran and cast its rays upon all regions. Ere long Iran shall become the envy of the world and the Iranians shall become the object of the world's admiration.

order.why: Read the further appreciation of the Parsis.
Explore the image of a renewed crown.
shortened: O friends of God! The Lord has once again placed a crown of royal jewels upon the head of the Parsees, hung a bejeweled necklace of divine bounty around their neck, and clothed them in a garment of endless grace, so that the sun of Iran's eternal glory may shine resplendent and the greatness of their ancestors may become manifest.

order.why: Place Persian and Zoroastrian devotion together.
Turn to the poetic life of Shiraz.
Read the reported appreciation of manners and hospitality in its historical setting.
Introduce the ideal of simplicity through the desert account.
shortened: The Arab of the desert teaches us a great lesson in the simple life. Living as he does in the waste Sahara he lacks all the means of life except a crude tent, a rug or mat, a caldron, a sword hanging to the inside pole of the tent and a javelin tied to the outside pole. This is all his furniture. Then, if he is wealthy he has a mare, or a horse, a few camels and maybe adjoining his tent a palm grove. It never occurs to his mind that there is anything else in this world. He is happy and has no worries.

order.why: Let the longer story test the attraction of wealth and urban splendor.
Retain the reported description of independence.
shortened: But Iranians are noble and passionate, unaccustomed to subjugation.

order.why: Examine the broad contrast drawn between religious and public life.
shortened: To the Occidental his God is - if he even acknowledges a God above him - a metaphysical Being in a remote, strange and nebulous beyond, to Whom one pays homage on Feasts and Holy Days, and Who does not count in every-day life, in commerce and politics, in general behaviour. But to the Oriental the Godhead is a real personality, present in everything and everywhere. Every-day life, the orders of nature, in brief the whole of human and animal life are the work of God, are subject to the Laws of God.

order.why: Consider the claim that spiritual ties sustain unity.
Read the hope for a higher civilization in the East.
Bring Japan’s progress and cooperation into the discussion.
Extend the outlook to China.
Revisit the reported contrast of simple and complex ways of life.
Return to appreciation for the Parsees’ service.
shortened: The Blessed Perfection expressed always great love for the Parsee friends.
The Zoroastrians of India have made great effort and served the Cause of God in the most unselfish manner.
The Parsees have demonstrated very praiseworthy exertions in the promotion of Truth and have lived with utmost joy and fragrance.

order.why: End with a historically worded hope for reciprocal learning between Iran and Germany.
Open with the hope that a cultural inheritance may benefit other peoples.

questions: How can the memory of a culture’s achievements become a responsibility for renewal rather than a reason for complacency?
What do the readings on poetry, hospitality, and justice suggest about the gifts a community can offer beyond its own borders?
How can we read broad historical contrasts between East and West attentively while avoiding assumptions about every member of a society?
What does the Qur’an’s invitation to mutual knowledge add to the selections’ hopes for cultural exchange?
How might a community preserve simplicity, devotion, or artistic inheritance while remaining open to change and learning from others?

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 49:13 · Peoples and mutual knowledge
references.note: The verse places human diversity within a common origin, invites mutual knowledge, and locates honor in righteousness. Read it beside the collection’s cultural appreciations and sweeping historical contrasts to explore the difference between valuing an inheritance and asserting superiority.
